title: intensive, motor, personalized, anywhere, challenging training for premanifest and early SpinoCerebellar Ataxia
summary:
Spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) is a rare, genetically caused neurodegenerative disorder that leads to progressive impairments in balance, coordination, and movement. Existing motor rehabilitation programs are primarily designed for patients in the moderate or advanced stages of the disease. In early stages, these programs often show only minimal effects, as the training requirements are not sufficiently challenging for individuals with mild or no symptoms. At the same time, studies in SCA animal models suggest that intensive motor training in the early phases of the disease can delay the onset of symptoms and reduce neuronal degeneration. This suggests that the early stages of SCA represent a therapeutic window that has not yet been fully utilized.
The impact pr/eSCA project aims to develop and evaluate a personalized, intensive training program for individuals with early-stage SCA as well as for presymptomatic mutation carriers. Thirty participants in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic stages of the disease will complete a six-week training program consisting of three sessions per week, each lasting 30–40 minutes. The training is designed as a home program and is individually adapted to participants’ motor abilities. The focus is on core stability and balance, with the difficulty level progressively increased to ensure a high but realistic training intensity. The six-week main training phase is followed by a 6-month follow-up period with individually documented training.  
The program’s effectiveness is assessed using clinical tests, digital motion analysis in the laboratory and in patients’ daily lives via wearable sensors, as well as patient-reported outcomes. Additionally, a blood biomarker of neuronal damage (neurofilament - NfL) is measured to investigate potential neuroprotective effects of the training.
The study aims to bring about a paradigm shift from purely symptom-oriented therapy to early, preventive intervention. In the long term, impact pr/eSCA—prospectively in combination with future neuroprotective gene therapies—could help slow the progression of the disease and preserve the independent mobility of those affected for longer.

interventions.name: We will assess the effectiveness of a 6-week intensive individualized home training protocol programme for participants in the premanifest or early stage of spinocerebellar ataxia. . The training period is preceded by a prior baseline period of six weeks, where participants receive standard care . P

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
First-degree relatives of an index patient with a known Spinocerebellar ataxia SCA 1, 2, 3, 6, or 27B mutation and a score of <8 on the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA).
Exclusion criteria:
Lack of informed consent, severe visual or hearing impairment, cognitive impairment, orthopedic limitations that impair mobility
